w: 1 Never monotherapy: antibiotics alone are not indicated; when they are Hint + final review · 8 questions in the bank Know this Antibiotics are always an adjunct to surgical and non-surgical therapy, given after SRP. Indications: acute infection with systemic signs, aggressive and refractory periodontitis. Know when antibiotics are indicated (always as an adjunct after SRP, never alone: acute infection with systemic signs, aggressive and refractory disease; local delivery for one breaking-down site in a stable maintenance patient), local vs systemic, and which ones the lecture recommends (the regimens on Dr. Litz's chart, the three local agents), with their cautions. When to consider antibiotics: an acute periodontal infection with systemic manifestations (fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy: a localized infection starting to spread); aggressive periodontitis, which hits young patients with severe attachment and bone loss in a short time and has to be treated aggressively; and refractory periodontitis, where a patient who has done everything asked (good home care, thorough SRP, surgery, 3-month maintenance) still loses attachment. And always as an adjunct to surgical and non-surgical therapy: "the use of systemic or locally delivered antibiotics is not to be used as a monotherapy in the treatment of periodontal disease." That was his main take-home message. 2 Biofilms: only mechanical debridement removes them; barrier, β-lactamase, slow growth A professor's hint · 4 questions in the bank Know this The dirty-pot analogy: rinses and water piks don't remove biofilm; mechanical debridement does. Biofilms resist antibiotics by a physical barrier, β-lactamase and a slower growth rate. Biofilms are insoluble and stuck to the root: rinses and water piks leave them. Antibiotics come only at the completion of Phase I, after debridement. The putative pathogens live in a biofilm, an aggregation of multiple microorganisms: if one microbial colony is a house, a biofilm is a subdivision in a protective bubble. Biofilms are a trait of supragingival and subgingival plaque. They protect and harbor the resident bacteria, let colonies survive harsh environments, and are insoluble, which makes them hard to remove: rinsing, water irrigation and mouthwashes leave them in place, like a dirty pot left soaking overnight that still has to be scrubbed. That is mechanical debridement: the patient's toothbrush and floss, and our curettes and ultrasonics. Some biofilm organisms survive antibiotic concentrations 500-1000 times greater than systemic delivery can reach. In class he called this the point to "star" and "know for life": the only way to get rid of a biofilm is mechanical debridement. A mouthrinse can supplement it, never replace it. Biofilms make bacteria resistant to antibiotics in three ways: (1) a physical barrier that makes antibiotic penetration difficult; (2) an increased concentration of beta-lactamase inside, which destroys the beta-lactam ring of our strongest antibiotics ("anytime you see -ase on the end of a word, that's what it destroys"); and (3) a slower growth rate of the resident bacteria, which makes them less susceptible to many antibiotics. 3 The host response does the damage: bacteria the key, the host the engine A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Bacteria are the key; the host response is the engine. Periodontal disease is not an autoimmune disease. Deeper pockets, more bacteria, a bigger response, more breakdown: a vicious cycle. His flowchart reads left to right, like a sentence. It always begins with the microbial challenge. Once plaque builds up along the gingival margin, the body recognizes it as foreign and mounts a host immune-inflammatory response, sending cells to destroy the bacteria, as it should. But the site turns into a war zone with collateral damage: while fighting the bacteria, our cells release pro-inflammatory cytokines and prostaglandins, which drive connective tissue and bone breakdown, seen as the clinical signs of disease: deeper pockets and bone loss. A deeper pocket is a niche for more bacteria; a bigger bacterial load calls for a bigger cellular response and more cytokines, which means more breakdown: a vicious cycle. The take-home: it always begins with bacteria. Periodontal disease is not an autoimmune disease; the body doesn't destroy itself without a stimulus. His analogy is the car in your garage. The engine (the host response) is what gets you from periodontal health to periodontal disease, but at two in the morning it won't start by itself. It sits there dormant until someone turns the key, and the key is the bacteria. 4 The cascade: pellicle, complement, neutrophils then macrophages, IL-1 A professor's hint · 6 questions in the bank Know this Pellicle within minutes; gram-positive cocci first, then the orange and red complexes. Complement calls in PMNs and releases histamine (edema). Neutrophils first (24-48 h), macrophages later. IL-1 (osteoclast activating factor): osteoclasts, collagenase, PGE2, MMPs. "You know these next two slides, you're going to have a pretty good understanding of the way periodontal disease works." How bacteria build up: a salivary pellicle forms within minutes of a prophylaxis and is the foundation that promotes bacterial adhesion (by the time the patient pays at the front desk, the foundation is laid). The first colonizers are mostly gram-positive cocci, fed by dietary proteins in saliva. As hygiene slips, plaque along the gingival margin inflames the soft tissue, which creates the environment for the late colonizers, the orange and then the red complexes, fed by blood and GCF. Colonization is sequential, not haphazard. The bacteria live in a biofilm, which protects them and works as a simple circulatory system, bringing nutrients and removing wastes. How the body fights back: the cascade starts with complement, a cluster of serum proteins whose primary function is to control inflammation. Complement can lyse bacterial cell membranes directly, but its main job is as a chemoattractant for phagocytes (PMNs). It also releases histamine from mast cells, which increases vascular permeability: fluid and cells leak into the tissue, and that is the edema of inflammation. Neutrophils (PMNs) are the first responders, like the paramedics at a wreck: they arrive within about 24-48 hours of a bacterial insult to remove foreign agents. If they can't keep up, macrophages arrive later. Both are good cells ("if you didn't have them, you'd be dead"), but both release cytokines, intercellular signals that regulate cellular activity, including immune function. 5 Bactericidal vs bacteriostatic; never combine one of each A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Bactericidal drugs only kill dividing bacteria; a bacteriostatic drug stops division. Amoxicillin + metronidazole works because both are bactericidal. Bacteriostatic agents inhibit the growth and reproduction of bacteria without killing them, so the body can finish the job. Bactericidal agents kill bacteria directly, but only bacteria that are actively dividing, a narrow window. That is why a biofilm's slower growth hurts our strongest antibiotics. It is also why, when two antibiotics are given at the same time, they must be both bactericidal or both bacteriostatic, never one of each: the bacteriostatic drug slows growth and shuts the bactericidal drug's only window. Antibiotics are classified by molecular structure and mechanism: they interrupt the synthesis of structural components or alter metabolic functions unique to microbial cells. Amoxicillin plus metronidazole: 375 mg amoxicillin tid plus 250 mg metronidazole tid, for 7 days. 6 Allergy, cephalosporin cross-reactivity and clindamycin A professor's hint · 7 questions in the bank Know this Upset stomach = side effect. Hives or difficulty breathing = true (anaphylactic) allergy: nothing from that class. 10-15% of adults report a penicillin allergy. Penicillin-allergic and unsure about cephalosporins: don't give one. Cephalosporin-allergic: move on to another class. Clindamycin is usually next (not with colitis). Hypersensitivity is the most common side effect; about 10-15% of adults are reported to have an allergic response to penicillin. Before handing over any prescription, get verbal confirmation that the patient isn't allergic to it. When a patient reports an allergy, ask what reaction they have. An upset stomach is a side effect, not an allergy. Hives or difficulty breathing (the throat closing) point to a true, potentially fatal anaphylactic reaction: then don't give that drug or anything in its class. Cephalosporins: beta-lactam compounds similar in structure and action to the penicillins; bactericidal by inhibiting cell wall synthesis. Grouped in generations (1st to 4th on the slide; a 5th exists) by spectrum and order of development: later generations move from mostly gram-positive toward gram-negative coverage and more resistance to beta-lactamase, so perio favors the later ones. Some evidence of increased bone penetration; may be given with food. About 10% cross-reactivity in patients allergic to penicillin: don't give one to a patient allergic to penicillin who is unsure about cephalosporins. As taught, a patient allergic to cephalosporins has a 100% chance of penicillin allergy, so move on to another class. Cephalosporins can also interfere with oral contraceptives and increase bleeding time with warfarin. 7 Interactions: warfarin, oral contraceptives, digoxin, alcohol A professor's hint · 7 questions in the bank Know this The two things to tell every metronidazole patient: orange-red urine, and a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol. His Van Gogh story (Starry Night halos = digoxin toxicity) is there to make one interaction stick: macrolides can raise digoxin levels. Macrolide interactions: they can raise plasma levels of, and potentiate, many drugs, including digoxin (risking digoxin toxicity), Dilantin, oral anticoagulants (warfarin), cyclosporine, midazolam, corticosteroids and theophylline. Digoxin, a positive inotrope for heart failure, has a narrow therapeutic range. His story: Van Gogh, given digoxin in an asylum, painted The Starry Night's halos around bright lights, a symptom of digoxin toxicity. Cautions: it increases the anticoagulant effect of warfarin (check with the physician); it may decrease the renal excretion of lithium; it is teratogenic, so avoid it in pregnancy. Tell every patient two things: their urine may turn orange-red, and alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction with an extreme headache, like Antabuse. No alcohol. 8 Local delivery: the stable maintenance site; PerioChip, Atridox, Arestin Hint + final review · 6 questions in the bank Know this Local delivery's real indication: one site breaking down in a stable maintenance patient, after debriding it. Not a dozen sites (they need surgery) and not aggressive periodontitis. Indications: localized sites that don't respond to Phase I (the textbook answer, "not a great indication"; generalized residual pockets need surgery, not a dozen expensive cartridges) and, the real indication, localized sites in an otherwise stable maintenance patient: one site that was 3 mm for years is now 5 mm and bleeding, a last attempt before surgery. Anesthetize, debride with the ultrasonic and hand instruments, then place the agent, and re-evaluate in 4-6 weeks. Not a replacement for conventional therapy, and not for aggressive periodontitis. PerioChip: 2.5 mg chlorhexidine in a gelatin matrix, 4 x 5 x 0.35 mm ("you don't need to know these dimensions"). Self-retentive on contact with moisture, inserted into the pocket at the end of SRP, biodegradable (no removal appointment). Release peaks about 2 hours after placement, then decreases over about 9 days. 9 Periostat: sub-antimicrobial doxycycline, collagenase, small added gains Review guide · 6 questions in the bank Know this Periostat (sub-antimicrobial doxycycline): 20 mg bid vs the antibiotic's 100 mg once a day. No antimicrobial activity, so no resistance and long-term use; inhibits collagenase from PMNs; the first FDA-approved systemic host modulator, an adjunct to SRP. Periostat is the first FDA-approved systemic (by mouth) drug for host modulation, used as an adjunct to scaling and root planing: the same rules apply, and the biofilm still has to be disrupted mechanically. It is a low, sub-antimicrobial dose of doxycycline (SDD). Doxycycline as an antibiotic is 100 mg once a day; Periostat is 20 mg twice a day (bid), a fifth of the dose. At that dose it has no antimicrobial activity (the bacteria take one look at it and leave it alone), so resistance is not evident and it can be given long-term. Its mechanism is to inhibit collagenase, particularly the collagenase made by the host's own cells such as PMNs, where most of the destruction happens. Take it 1 hour before or 2 hours after a meal and avoid calcium-containing products. It is contraindicated with hypersensitivity to doxycycline or other tetracyclines, in pregnant or lactating women, and in children under 12. Does it work? Many studies say yes. His example is Caton et al., 2000, a randomized, multicenter, double-blind trial. Both groups had periodontitis and got the same SRP; one then took a placebo, the other Periostat 20 mg bid, for nine months, with re-evaluations at 3, 6 and 9 months. The Periostat group had statistically significant extra pocket reduction at every visit (4-6 mm pockets: 0.95 mm with Periostat vs 0.69 mm with placebo at 9 months; 7 mm or deeper: 1.68 vs 1.2 mm) and the same pattern in attachment gain (1.03 vs 0.86 mm; 1.35 vs 1.17 mm). He said not to learn this study's numbers, just what it shows: statistically significant, but is it clinically significant? These are fractions of a millimeter. It helps where we need all the help we can get, in refractory and aggressive periodontitis. Efficacy beyond 9 months and safety beyond 12 months haven't been established, and the net changes were limited. The AAP: adjunctive therapies (systemic antibiotics, local antibiotics, Periostat) are not a substitute for mechanical debridement, meticulous home care and the other therapies that reduce the bacterial load. 10 NSAIDs, bisphosphonates and BRONJ; why to step lightly Review guide · 10 questions in the bank NSAIDs such as aspirin and ibuprofen inhibit the formation of prostaglandins, including PGE2, which neutrophils, macrophages, fibroblasts and gingival epithelial cells make in response to bacteria. PGE2 upregulates osteoclasts and bone resorption, so blocking it is a "pretty good first step." Given daily for up to 3 years, NSAIDs slowed alveolar bone destruction, but daily dosing is necessary: one dose, or a week or two, does nothing. That is the problem, because prolonged NSAID use causes GI problems (a bad gastric ulcer can do serious damage), hemorrhage from decreased platelet aggregation, and renal or hepatic impairment. "We can't just blindly start prescribing NSAIDs" to every periodontal patient, so long-term NSAID use for host modulation hasn't developed. Bisphosphonates are not new drugs. They are bone-seeking agents that inhibit bone resorption by inhibiting osteoclasts, may have anticollagenase effects too, and some studies show changes in white blood cell counts. At first glance, "we just found the magic bullet." The catch is bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (BRONJ): bone necrosis after an invasive dental procedure (a simple extraction or periodontal surgery counts), with some reports of it happening spontaneously. These drugs are common, given mostly to older women for osteoporosis, by mouth or in high-dose IV forms, and most complications are with the high-dose IV forms. 11 Drug by drug: mechanism, ANUG, C. diff, tetracycline cautions, food Core of the slides · 11 questions in the bank A derivative of lincomycin. It reversibly binds the 50S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting protein synthesis; usually bactericidal, bacteriostatic depending on drug concentration, infection site and organism. Effective against a wide range of periodontal bacteria and the usual first choice for a patient with a true allergy to penicillins and cephalosporins. Dose: 150-300 mg po tid for 7 days. Its known side effect is pseudomembranous colitis: altered gut flora let Clostridium difficile (C. diff) overgrow, which can be fatal. The condition is reported with other antibiotics too, but clindamycin "gets a bad rap" for it. Avoid it in patients with a history of colitis. Effective only against obligate anaerobes, particularly spirochetes. It reacts with bacterial DNA, inhibiting DNA replication, and is almost always bactericidal. Useful in aggressive periodontitis and ANUG (acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis). Often combined with amoxicillin to widen the spectrum, with highly effective results: both are bactericidal, so they can be given together. 250 mg tid. Food delays but doesn't reduce absorption; bacterial resistance is low. 12 Augmentin, erythromycin, macrolides, pregnancy Core of the slides · 6 questions in the bank Augmentin combines amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, a beta-lactamase inhibitor: it "inactivates their inactivator," so the amoxicillin can work. Effective against gram-positive and more gram-negative organisms, including anaerobes; useful in aggressive or refractory periodontitis. It may cause more GI upset (so give it with food) and is significantly more expensive than other penicillins. Written as 500 or 875 mg (the amoxicillin dose); the clavulanic acid stays 125 mg either way. Clarithromycin (Biaxin): well absorbed with or without food. It has caused fetal abnormalities in animals and is pregnancy category C: avoid it in pregnant women. 250-500 mg po q12h (bid). ("If there's ever an award for the best smelling antibiotic, this wins": vanilla.) Also flagged in class Bacteria (plaque) are the primary etiologic factor. Smoking and diabetes compound it but can't cause it alone. Antibiotics (via vitamin K-producing gut flora) and metronidazole raise warfarin's effect. You can prescribe; tell the physician and let them decide. Erythromycin: high resistance and near-universal GI upset. Azithromycin and clarithromycin cover anaerobes better. Said again in the Nov 5 class: bacteria (plaque) are the primary etiologic factor. And "definitely know this one": antibiotics alone are not indicated. Gram-negative bacteria are required but not sufficient: the host response to them does most of the damage. Why host modulation goes slowly: turn the host response down too far and an innocent infection could turn lethal. BRONJ: scraping the necrotic bone is trauma, the very cause, so lesions grow. Bisphosphonates stay in the system for years; most complications are with high-dose IV. No bisphosphonate is approved for periodontal disease. You can skip PerioChip's dimensions aren't worth memorizing; know its content (2.5 mg chlorhexidine in gelatin), that it's self-retentive and biodegradable, and the 2-hour peak. Superseded for the final: at the Nov 12 review Dr. Abou-Arraj said not to focus on learning the doses (writing prescriptions is tested in the spring), so the questions that asked for a dose came out of the Question Bank. For reference, Dr. Litz's chart: Augmentin 250-500 mg tid × 10 days; amoxicillin 375 + metronidazole 250 mg tid × 7 days; clindamycin 150-300 mg qid × 10 days; doxycycline 100 mg bid day 1, then 100 mg a day, × 10-14 days; metronidazole 250 mg tid-qid × 10 days; minocycline 200 mg bid day 1, then 100 mg bid, × 10-14 days; tetracycline 250 mg qid × 14-21 days. Metronidazole regimens: not under 16. And the drug slides' doses. Caton 2000: SRP + Periostat beat SRP + placebo at 3, 6 and 9 months, statistically significant but by fractions of a millimeter. Know the point (is it clinically significant?), not the numbers. The doses aren't the point of the final, though Dr. Litz said in class to know his chart; Dr. Abou-Arraj's word at the final's review came later. A question may show a dose, but it won't ask whether the dose is right. The questions that asked for a dose came out of the Question Bank; the chart stays in the notes and Review.
